claim: The H. neptunium chromosome contains two open reading frames that encode bactofilin homologs, HNE_0444 and HNE_2629.
source: The H. neptunium chromosome contains two open reading frames that encode bactofilin homologs, HNE_0444 and HNE_2629 (Badger et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Badger et al., 2006, which provides external evidence for the presence of these genes.

claim: HNE_2629 is a potential ortholog of C. crescentus BacA with 43% identity and 60% similarity.
source: Reciprocal BLAST searches identified HNE_2629 as a potential ortholog of C. crescentus BacA (43% identity, 60% similarity), whereas HNE_0444 was only distantly related (<30% identity) to other so-far characterized bactofilin homologs.
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis (BLAST searches) performed by the authors, which constitutes data-driven evidence.

claim: HNE_0444 was only distantly related (<30% identity) to other characterized bactofilin homologs.
source: Reciprocal BLAST searches identified HNE_2629 as a potential ortholog of C. crescentus BacA (43% identity, 60% similarity), whereas HNE_0444 was only distantly related (<30% identity) to other so-far characterized bactofilin homologs.
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis (BLAST searches) performed by the authors.

claim: The two bactofilin homologs of H. neptunium are designated BacA (HNE_2629) and BacD (HNE_0444).
source: Based on these results, we propose to designate the two bactofilin homologs of H. neptunium BacA (HNE_2629) and BacD (HNE_0444), respectively.
evidence: This is a nomenclature proposal based on the authors' analysis and inference from sequence similarity data.

claim: bacA forms a putative bicistronic operon with lmdC.
source: bacA forms a putative bicistronic operon with lmdC, an essential gene encoding an M23 peptidase homolog (Cserti et al., 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cserti et al., 2017, and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: lmdC is an essential gene encoding an M23 peptidase homolog.
source: bacA forms a putative bicistronic operon with lmdC, an essential gene encoding an M23 peptidase homolog (Cserti et al., 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cserti et al., 2017.

claim: The bacA and lmdC genes overlap by 17 base pairs.
source: The two genes overlap by 17 base pairs, suggesting that their expression is closely coupled.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence analysis, which is data-driven evidence.

claim: The overlap of bacA and lmdC suggests that their expression is closely coupled.
source: The two genes overlap by 17 base pairs, suggesting that their expression is closely coupled.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene overlap.

claim: bacD is not part of an operon.
source: bacD, by contrast, is not part of an operon.
evidence: This is a direct observation from genomic analysis.

claim: Both BacA and BacD display the typical architecture of bactofilins, with a central polymerization domain flanked by short non-structured N- and C-terminal regions.
source: Both BacA and BacD display the typical architecture of bactofilins, with a central polymerization domain flanked by short non-structured N- and C-terminal regions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The ΔbacA and ΔbacAD cells showed severe morphological defects.
source: The ΔbacA and ΔbacAD cells showed severe morphological defects, as reflected by irregularly shaped, elongated and/or oversized cells, buds directly fused with the mother cell body, branched stalks, and multiple wide protrusions that emerged from the cells in an apparently random fashion (Figure 1C–E), reminiscent of the pseudostalks reported for a bactofilin-deficient A. biprosthecum mutant (Caccamo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 1C-E and is compared to a cited study (Caccamo et al., 2020).

claim: The morphological defects in ΔbacA and ΔbacAD cells include irregularly shaped, elongated and/or oversized cells, buds directly fused with the mother cell body, branched stalks, and multiple wide protrusions.
source: The ΔbacA and ΔbacAD cells showed severe morphological defects, as reflected by irregularly shaped, elongated and/or oversized cells, buds directly fused with the mother cell body, branched stalks, and multiple wide protrusions that emerged from the cells in an apparently random fashion (Figure 1C–E), reminiscent of the pseudostalks reported for a bactofilin-deficient A. biprosthecum mutant (Caccamo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a detailed description of observed phenotypes from microscopy data.

claim: The morphological defects in ΔbacA and ΔbacAD cells are reminiscent of the pseudostalks reported for a bactofilin-deficient A. biprosthecum mutant.
source: The ΔbacA and ΔbacAD cells showed severe morphological defects, as reflected by irregularly shaped, elongated and/or oversized cells, buds directly fused with the mother cell body, branched stalks, and multiple wide protrusions that emerged from the cells in an apparently random fashion (Figure 1C–E), reminiscent of the pseudostalks reported for a bactofilin-deficient A. biprosthecum mutant (Caccamo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on the authors' data and a cited study.

claim: The growth defects in ΔbacA and ΔbacAD cells did not have any major effects on the doubling time.
source: Surprisingly, these growth defects did not have any major defects on the doubling time (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The wild-type phenotype could be largely restored by expressing an ectopic copy of bacA under the control of a copper-inducible promoter.
source: The wild-type phenotype could be largely restored by expressing an ectopic copy of bacA under the control of a copper-inducible promoter, even though BacA accumulated to lower-than-normal levels under this condition, confirming the absence of polar effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is a complementation experiment demonstrating functional rescue, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: BacA accumulated to lower-than-normal levels when expressed from a copper-inducible promoter.
source: The wild-type phenotype could be largely restored by expressing an ectopic copy of bacA under the control of a copper-inducible promoter, even though BacA accumulated to lower-than-normal levels under this condition, confirming the absence of polar effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is an observation from immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The complementation of ΔbacA confirms the absence of polar effects.
source: The wild-type phenotype could be largely restored by expressing an ectopic copy of bacA under the control of a copper-inducible promoter, even though BacA accumulated to lower-than-normal levels under this condition, confirming the absence of polar effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is an inference from the complementation experiment.

claim: The deletion of bacD did not cause any obvious cell shape defects.
source: The deletion of bacD, by contrast, did not cause any obvious cell shape defects (Figure 1C, E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy and quantitative analysis shown in the cited figures.

claim: Neither bacD deletion nor bacD overexpression had any influence on the proportion of distorted or amorphous cells in the ΔbacA background.
source: Moreover, neither bacD deletion nor bacD overexpression had any influence on the proportion of distorted or amorphous cells in the ΔbacA background (Figure 1C and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and F).
evidence: This is an observation from quantitative analysis of cell morphology shown in the cited figures.

claim: BacA has a critical role in the regulation of cell growth in H. neptunium.
source: These results demonstrate that BacA has a critical role in the regulation of cell growth in H. neptunium, whereas BacD might be an auxiliary factor of so-far unknown function, similar to BacB in C. crescentus (Kühn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant phenotype data and complementation experiments, with a comparison to a cited study.

claim: BacD might be an auxiliary factor of so-far unknown function, similar to BacB in C. crescentus.
source: These results demonstrate that BacA has a critical role in the regulation of cell growth in H. neptunium, whereas BacD might be an auxiliary factor of so-far unknown function, similar to BacB in C. crescentus (Kühn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the lack of phenotype for bacD deletion and comparison to a cited study.

claim: Following BacA depletion, stalk formation initially proceeded as in the wild-type strain.
source: Following cells at the swimmer-to-stalked cell transition, we observed that stalk formation initially proceeded as in the wild-type strain.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse microscopy experiments.

claim: As BacA was gradually depleted, stalk elongation ceased and the stalk structure started to widen and eventually develop multiple bulges.
source: However, as BacA was gradually depleted, stalk elongation ceased and the stalk structure started to widen and eventually develop multiple bulges that kept on expanding in an apparently uncontrolled manner.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: BacA appears to be required to maintain the polar growth zone at the stalk base.
source: Thus, BacA appears to be required to maintain the polar growth zone at the stalk base, with its absence leading to unconstrained growth of the stalk cell wall.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed phenotypes upon BacA depletion.

claim: The absence of BacA leads to unconstrained growth of the stalk cell wall.
source: Thus, BacA appears to be required to maintain the polar growth zone at the stalk base, with its absence leading to unconstrained growth of the stalk cell wall.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed phenotypes upon BacA depletion.

claim: In the ΔbacAD mutant, cells started growth by the formation of irregularly shaped stalks that started to branch.
source: In this setup, cells again started growth by the formation of irregularly shaped stalks that started to branch, with branches developing either into extensive hyphal-like structures or large, amorphous compartments that may represent morphologically aberrant buds.
evidence: This is an observation from flow-cell time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: Branches in ΔbacAD cells developed either into extensive hyphal-like structures or large, amorphous compartments that may represent morphologically aberrant buds.
source: In this setup, cells again started growth by the formation of irregularly shaped stalks that started to branch, with branches developing either into extensive hyphal-like structures or large, amorphous compartments that may represent morphologically aberrant buds.
evidence: This is an observation from flow-cell time-lapse microscopy with speculative interpretation.

claim: At irregular intervals, ΔbacAD cells divided at the junctions between hyphal and bulged cellular segments, releasing smaller amorphous fragments and, occasionally, also cells with close-to-normal morphology.
source: At irregular intervals, cells divided at the junctions between hyphal and bulged cellular segments, releasing smaller amorphous fragments and, occasionally, also cells with close-to-normal morphology.
evidence: This is an observation from flow-cell time-lapse microscopy.

claim: Wild-type cells showed the usual growth pattern when cultivated in flow-cell conditions.
source: Wild-type cells, by contrast, showed the usual growth pattern when cultivated under these conditions (Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from flow-cell time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 2—video 2.

claim: Wild-type cells showed the typical succession of growth modes: dispersed growth in swimmer cells, zonal growth at the stalk base in stalked cells, and localized dispersed growth in the nascent bud.
source: Wild-type cells showed the typical succession of growth modes, with dispersed growth in swimmer cells, zonal growth at the stalk base in stalked cells, and localized dispersed growth in the nascent bud (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from HADA pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the ΔbacAD background, the switch in growth modes was abolished.
source: In the ΔbacAD background, by contrast, this switch in the growth modes was abolished.
evidence: This is an observation from HADA pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ΔbacAD cells with close-to-normal morphology that had just initiated stalk formation still showed a distinct fluorescent focus at the stalked pole.
source: Cells with close-to-normal morphology that had just initiated stalk formation still showed a distinct fluorescent focus at the stalked pole, suggesting that the initial recruitment of the machinery responsible for stalk formation occurred in a bactofilin-independent manner.
evidence: This is an observation from HADA pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The initial recruitment of the machinery responsible for stalk formation occurred in a bactofilin-independent manner.
source: Cells with close-to-normal morphology that had just initiated stalk formation still showed a distinct fluorescent focus at the stalked pole, suggesting that the initial recruitment of the machinery responsible for stalk formation occurred in a bactofilin-independent manner.
evidence: This is an inference from the HADA labeling pattern in early-stage ΔbacAD cells.

claim: All other ΔbacAD cell types, including amorphous cells with aberrant stalk- and bud-like extensions, only displayed diffuse fluorescence.
source: However, all other cell types, including amorphous cells with aberrant stalk- and bud-like extensions, only displayed diffuse fluorescence, which points to uncontrolled growth by dispersed incorporation of new peptidoglycan throughout the entire cell envelope.
evidence: This is an observation from HADA pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The diffuse fluorescence in ΔbacAD cells points to uncontrolled growth by dispersed incorporation of new peptidoglycan throughout the entire cell envelope.
source: However, all other cell types, including amorphous cells with aberrant stalk- and bud-like extensions, only displayed diffuse fluorescence, which points to uncontrolled growth by dispersed incorporation of new peptidoglycan throughout the entire cell envelope.
evidence: This is an inference from the HADA labeling pattern.

claim: The bactofilin cytoskeleton is required to limit cell wall biosynthesis to the different growth zones of H. neptunium.
source: These findings support the notion that the bactofilin cytoskeleton is required to limit cell wall biosynthesis to the different growth zones of H. neptunium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HADA labeling experiments and observed phenotypes.

claim: The ΔbacA and ΔbacAD mutants showed close-to-normal growth rates despite severe cell shape defects.
source: Despite their severe cell shape defects, the ΔbacA and ΔbacAD mutants showed close-to-normal growth rates.
evidence: This is an observation from growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Muropeptide analysis revealed that the global composition of peptidoglycan in ΔbacA and ΔbacAD mutants remained essentially unchanged.
source: Moreover, muropeptide analysis revealed that the global composition of their peptidoglycan remained essentially unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an observation from HPLC analysis of muropeptides shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BacA might affect cell wall composition at a local scale or act mainly by modulating the activity of the generic cell elongation machinery.
source: These findings suggested that BacA might affect cell wall composition at a local scale or act mainly by modulating the activity of the generic cell elongation machinery.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the normal growth rates and unchanged global peptidoglycan composition.

claim: A model of the structure of BacA generated with AlphaFold-Multimer suggested that the protein adopted a β-helical fold.
source: A model of the structure of BacA generated with AlphaFold-Multimer (Evans et al., 2022) suggested that the protein adopted a β-helical fold and polymerized through head-to-head and tail-to-tail interactions between different subunits (Figure 3A), as revealed previously in experimental studies (Deng et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling (AlphaFold-Multimer) cited to Evans et al., 2022, and is consistent with previous experimental studies cited.

claim: The AlphaFold-Multimer model suggested that BacA polymerized through head-to-head and tail-to-tail interactions between different subunits.
source: A model of the structure of BacA generated with AlphaFold-Multimer (Evans et al., 2022) suggested that the protein adopted a β-helical fold and polymerized through head-to-head and tail-to-tail interactions between different subunits (Figure 3A), as revealed previously in experimental studies (Deng et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling consistent with previous experimental studies cited.

claim: Purified BacA produced a mixture of long filaments, filament bundles and two-dimensional polymeric sheets in vitro.
source: Consistent with this prediction, purified BacA produced a mixture of long filaments, filament bundles and two-dimensional polymeric sheets in vitro, which could be readily visualized by transmission electron microscopy (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from transmission electron microscopy shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upon heterologous co-expression in E. coli, fluorescently tagged derivatives of BacA and BacD co-localized into extended filamentous structures that were associated with the cell envelope.
source: Moreover, upon heterologous co-expression in Escherichia coli, fluorescently tagged derivatives of BacA and BacD co-localized into extended filamentous structures that were associated with the cell envelope (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The BacA fusion formed qualitatively similar structures when produced alone in E. coli.
source: The BacA fusion formed qualitatively similar structures when produced alone, whereas the BacD fusion condensed into tight foci in the absence of BacA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The BacD fusion condensed into tight foci in the absence of BacA in E. coli.
source: The BacA fusion formed qualitatively similar structures when produced alone, whereas the BacD fusion condensed into tight foci in the absence of BacA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BacA and BacD interact with each other in vivo.
source: These results confirm the polymeric nature of bactofilin assemblies in H. neptunium and suggest that BacA and BacD interact with each other in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference from the co-localization experiments in E. coli.

claim: BacA-YFP was localized to the new cell pole in swimmer cells.
source: Time-lapse microscopy analysis of cells producing a BacA-YFP fusion on agarose pads (Figure 4A) revealed that the protein was localized to the new cell pole in swimmer cells and remained associated with the stalk base during the initial phase of stalk formation.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BacA-YFP remained associated with the stalk base during the initial phase of stalk formation.
source: Time-lapse microscopy analysis of cells producing a BacA-YFP fusion on agarose pads (Figure 4A) revealed that the protein was localized to the new cell pole in swimmer cells and remained associated with the stalk base during the initial phase of stalk formation.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At some point, BacA-YFP appeared to attach to the stalk structure and then move away from the base as new cell wall material was inserted.
source: At some point, it appeared to attach to the stalk structure and then move away from the base as new cell wall material was inserted.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Subsequently, stalk elongation ceased and the terminal stalk segment, delimited by the bactofilin assembly, started to swell and develop into a bud.
source: Subsequently, stalk elongation ceased and the terminal stalk segment, delimited by the bactofilin assembly, started to swell and develop into a bud, gradually displacing BacA-YFP in the direction of the stalk base as its size increased.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: After cell division, both the mother cell and the newborn swimmer cells showed a fluorescent focus.
source: After cell division, both the mother cell and the newborn swimmer cells showed a fluorescent focus, indicating that the bactofilin assembly was split during cell division.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The bactofilin assembly was split during cell division.
source: After cell division, both the mother cell and the newborn swimmer cells showed a fluorescent focus, indicating that the bactofilin assembly was split during cell division.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of fluorescent foci in both daughter cells.

claim: Cell division occurred at a small distance from the BacA-YFP focus, leaving a short stalk-terminal segment in between the bactofilin assembly and the stalk tip.
source: We observed that cell division occurred at a small distance from the BacA-YFP focus, leaving a short stalk-terminal segment in between the bactofilin assembly and the stalk tip.
evidence: This is an observation from flow-cell time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—videos 1–3.

claim: After cytokinesis, the stalk elongated again prior to the initiation of the next budding event.
source: After cytokinesis, the stalk elongated again prior to the initiation of the next budding event.
evidence: This is an observation from flow-cell time-lapse microscopy.

claim: BacA-YFP was only occasionally detected at the stalked pole during the stalk restoration phase.
source: Notably, BacA-YFP was only occasionally detected at the stalked pole during the stalk restoration phase, suggesting that the bactofilin cytoskeleton no longer plays a major role in stalk growth once the stalk structure has been established.
evidence: This is an observation from flow-cell time-lapse microscopy.

claim: The bactofilin cytoskeleton no longer plays a major role in stalk growth once the stalk structure has been established.
source: Notably, BacA-YFP was only occasionally detected at the stalked pole during the stalk restoration phase, suggesting that the bactofilin cytoskeleton no longer plays a major role in stalk growth once the stalk structure has been established.
evidence: This is an inference from the localization pattern of BacA-YFP during stalk restoration.

claim: A demographic analysis confirmed that BacA-YFP localizes to the new cell pole in swimmer cells, remains at the stalk base in cells with short stalks, and then moves to a position close to the distal end of the stalk before the onset of budding.
source: A demographic analysis confirmed that the protein localizes to the new cell pole in swimmer cells, remains at the stalk base in cells with short stalks, and then moves to a position close to the distal end of the stalk before the onset of budding, remaining associated with the bud neck up to the point of cell division (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of fluorescence localization shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BacA-YFP remains associated with the bud neck up to the point of cell division.
source: A demographic analysis confirmed that the protein localizes to the new cell pole in swimmer cells, remains at the stalk base in cells with short stalks, and then moves to a position close to the distal end of the stalk before the onset of budding, remaining associated with the bud neck up to the point of cell division (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of fluorescence localization shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A BacD-Venus fusion showed a very similar localization behavior to BacA-YFP.
source: A very similar behavior was observed for a BacD variant fused to the yellow fluorescent protein Venus (Nagai et al., 2002; Figure 4C), consistent with the notion that the two bactofilin paralogs interact.
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The similar localization behavior of BacA-YFP and BacD-Venus is consistent with the notion that the two bactofilin paralogs interact.
source: A very similar behavior was observed for a BacD variant fused to the yellow fluorescent protein Venus (Nagai et al., 2002; Figure 4C), consistent with the notion that the two bactofilin paralogs interact.
evidence: This is an inference from the co-localization pattern.

claim: BacA and BacD co-localized to a large extent during all stages of the developmental cycle.
source: In support of this hypothesis, studies of a strain in which both proteins were fluorescently labeled showed that BacA and BacD indeed co-localized to a large extent during all stages of the developmental cycle (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from dual-color fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: At the onset of bud formation, the signals of BacA and BacD were not always fully superimposable.
source: However, at the onset of bud formation, the signals of the two proteins were not always fully superimposable, with BacD assemblies occasionally detectable both at the bud neck and in the mother cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from dual-color fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the absence of BacA, BacD-Venus still formed distinct foci, albeit at apparently random positions within the cell.
source: In the absence of BacA, BacD-Venus still formed distinct foci, albeit at apparently random positions within the cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: A BacA-YFP variant carrying the F130R mutation was evenly distributed in the cell and unable to functionally replace the wild-type protein.
source: Notably, a BacA-YFP variant carrying a previously reported mutation that disrupts the polymerization interface (F130R) (Deng et al., 2019; Vasa et al., 2015; Zuckerman et al., 2015) was evenly distributed in the cell and unable to functionally replace the wild-type protein, indicating that the formation of polymeric assemblies is essential for proper BacA localization and function (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy and phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6, with the mutation cited from previous studies.

claim: The formation of polymeric assemblies is essential for proper BacA localization and function.
source: Notably, a BacA-YFP variant carrying a previously reported mutation that disrupts the polymerization interface (F130R) (Deng et al., 2019; Vasa et al., 2015; Zuckerman et al., 2015) was evenly distributed in the cell and unable to functionally replace the wild-type protein, indicating that the formation of polymeric assemblies is essential for proper BacA localization and function (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is an inference from the phenotype of the F130R mutant.

claim: The bactofilin cytoskeleton might serve to limit the cell wall biosynthetic machinery to the different growth zones of H. neptunium.
source: Given that the bactofilin assemblies are localized to the boundaries of the stalk and the bud and required to prevent unconstrained growth of these cellular structures, we hypothesized that the bactofilin cytoskeleton might serve to limit the cell wall biosynthetic machinery to the different growth zones of H. neptunium.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the localization and mutant phenotype data.

claim: In the wild-type background, YFP-RodZ formed dynamic foci in the mother cell, at the (incipient) stalk base and the nascent bud.
source: In the wild-type background, YFP-RodZ formed dynamic foci in the mother cell, at the (incipient) stalk base and the nascent bud (Figure 5 and Figure 5—videos 1 and 2), thus localizing to the different growth zones detected by HADA labeling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—videos 1 and 2.

claim: YFP-RodZ localizes to the different growth zones detected by HADA labeling.
source: In the wild-type background, YFP-RodZ formed dynamic foci in the mother cell, at the (incipient) stalk base and the nascent bud (Figure 5 and Figure 5—videos 1 and 2), thus localizing to the different growth zones detected by HADA labeling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a comparison of YFP-RodZ localization with HADA labeling patterns.

claim: The elongasome is a key determinant of cell growth in H. neptunium.
source: These results are in line with previous findings identifying the elongasome as a key determinant of cell growth in H. neptunium (Cserti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion consistent with a cited previous study.

claim: YFP-RodZ foci were never observed in the stalk.
source: Importantly, however, YFP-RodZ foci were never observed in the stalk, suggesting that elongasome complexes are unable to cross the stalk base and the bud neck, even though their free components appear to be able to diffuse through the stalk to facilitate the de novo assembly of elongasomes in the incipient bud compartment.
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 5.

claim: Elongasome complexes are unable to cross the stalk base and the bud neck.
source: Importantly, however, YFP-RodZ foci were never observed in the stalk, suggesting that elongasome complexes are unable to cross the stalk base and the bud neck, even though their free components appear to be able to diffuse through the stalk to facilitate the de novo assembly of elongasomes in the incipient bud compartment.
evidence: This is an inference from the absence of YFP-RodZ foci in the stalk.

claim: Free components of the elongasome appear to be able to diffuse through the stalk to facilitate the de novo assembly of elongasomes in the incipient bud compartment.
source: Importantly, however, YFP-RodZ foci were never observed in the stalk, suggesting that elongasome complexes are unable to cross the stalk base and the bud neck, even though their free components appear to be able to diffuse through the stalk to facilitate the de novo assembly of elongasomes in the incipient bud compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to explain how elongasomes appear in the bud despite not being observed in the stalk.

claim: In the ΔbacAD mutant, the localization behavior of YFP-RodZ resembled that in the wild-type background in early stages of the cell cycle.
source: In the ΔbacAD mutant, the localization behavior of YFP-RodZ resembled that in the wild-type background as long as the cells were the early stages of the cell cycle, with dynamic foci detectable throughout the cell envelope and at the (future) stalk base (Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 3).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 3.

claim: At later stages in the ΔbacAD mutant, the elongasome was no longer excluded from the nascent stalk structure.
source: However, at later stages, the elongasome was no longer excluded from the nascent stalk structure and, in many cases, even appeared to be enriched this region, leading to its remodeling into an increasingly amorphous cellular extension (Figure 5 and Figure 5—videos 3–5).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—videos 3–5.

claim: In the ΔbacAD mutant, the elongasome appeared to be enriched in the nascent stalk region, leading to its remodeling into an increasingly amorphous cellular extension.
source: However, at later stages, the elongasome was no longer excluded from the nascent stalk structure and, in many cases, even appeared to be enriched this region, leading to its remodeling into an increasingly amorphous cellular extension (Figure 5 and Figure 5—videos 3–5).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—videos 3–5.

claim: The bactofilin cytoskeleton itself or the high degree of positive inner cell curvature induced in its presence at the stalk base appear to act as a barrier that excludes elongasome complexes from the stalk.
source: The bactofilin cytoskeleton itself or the high degree of positive inner cell curvature induced in its presence at the stalk base thus appear to act as a barrier that excludes elongasome complexes from the stalk and thus facilitates proper morphogenesis and bud development.
evidence: This is an inference from the YFP-RodZ localization patterns in wild-type and mutant cells.

claim: The mobility of BacA-YFP molecules decreased gradually from the swimmer over the stalked cell to the budding cell stage.
source: When calculating the average mean squared displacement of the tracked BacA-YFP molecules, we found that their mobility decreased gradually from the swimmer over the stalked cell to the budding cell stage (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from single-molecule tracking experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For each cell type, the distribution of step sizes in the single-particle tracks suggests the existence of two distinct diffusion regimes, with a static and a mobile population.
source: For each cell type, the distribution of step sizes in the single-particle tracks suggests the existence of two distinct diffusion regimes, with a static (D=0.02 ± 0.0004 µm2 s–1) and a mobile (D=0.35 ± 0.004 µm2 s–1) population, likely representing the polymerized and freely diffusible states, respectively (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an analysis of single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The static population of BacA-YFP likely represents the polymerized state.
source: For each cell type, the distribution of step sizes in the single-particle tracks suggests the existence of two distinct diffusion regimes, with a static (D=0.02 ± 0.0004 µm2 s–1) and a mobile (D=0.35 ± 0.004 µm2 s–1) population, likely representing the polymerized and freely diffusible states, respectively (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the diffusion analysis.

claim: The mobile population of BacA-YFP likely represents the freely diffusible state.
source: For each cell type, the distribution of step sizes in the single-particle tracks suggests the existence of two distinct diffusion regimes, with a static (D=0.02 ± 0.0004 µm2 s–1) and a mobile (D=0.35 ± 0.004 µm2 s–1) population, likely representing the polymerized and freely diffusible states, respectively (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the diffusion analysis.

claim: In swimmer cells, the static fraction of BacA-YFP comprised only ~60% of the molecules.
source: In swimmer cells, the static fraction comprised only ~60% of the molecules.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule tracking analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The proportion of static BacA-YFP molecules increased to ~70% in stalked cells.
source: Its proportion increased to ~70% in stalked cells and finally reached ~80% in budding cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule tracking analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The proportion of static BacA-YFP molecules reached ~80% in budding cells.
source: Its proportion increased to ~70% in stalked cells and finally reached ~80% in budding cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule tracking analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The F130R variant of BacA-YFP showed less than 15% of static molecules.
source: The F130R variant, by contrast, showed less than 15% of static molecules (Figure 6B and C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—video 1) consistent with the notion that it is impaired in polymerization but still able to assemble to some extent after undergoing a structural change that generates an alternative polymerization interface (Deng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from single-molecule tracking analysis shown in Figure 6B and C, with interpretation based on a cited study.

claim: The F130R variant is impaired in polymerization but still able to assemble to some extent after undergoing a structural change that generates an alternative polymerization interface.
source: The F130R variant, by contrast, showed less than 15% of static molecules (Figure 6B and C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—video 1) consistent with the notion that it is impaired in polymerization but still able to assemble to some extent after undergoing a structural change that generates an alternative polymerization interface (Deng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the diffusion data and a cited study (Deng et al., 2019).

claim: In H. neptunium, the assembly state of the bactofilin cytoskeleton changes as cells progress through their developmental cycle.
source: Collectively, these results show that, in H. neptunium, the assembly state of the bactofilin cytoskeleton changes as cells progress through their developmental cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the single-molecule tracking experiments.

claim: All cell types display a sizeable fraction of mobile BacA-YFP molecules, which could potentially reflect the dynamic reorganization of bactofilin assemblies during cell growth.
source: Moreover, despite the inherent stability of bactofilin polymers, all cell types display a sizeable fraction of mobile BacA-YFP molecules, which could potentially reflect the dynamic reorganization of bactofilin assemblies during cell growth.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the single-molecule tracking data.

claim: In several species in which bactofilins play a role in cell shape determination, the corresponding bactofilin genes are located adjacent to genes encoding putative M23 peptidases homologous to LmdC.
source: Notably, in several species in which bactofilins play a role in cell shape determination, the corresponding bactofilin genes are located adjacent to genes encoding putative M23 peptidases homologous to LmdC (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an observation from genomic analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A comprehensive bioinformatic analysis identified a total of 226 species from a wide variety of bacterial phyla with bactofilin genes located immediately upstream or downstream of open reading frames encoding proteins with a predicted M23 peptidase domain.
source: This analysis identified a total of 226 species from a wide variety of bacterial phyla (Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting a conserved functional association between bactofilins and M23 peptidases.
evidence: This is a result from a bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: The co-occurrence of bactofilin and M23 peptidase genes suggests a conserved functional association between bactofilins and M23 peptidases.
source: This analysis identified a total of 226 species from a wide variety of bacterial phyla (Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting a conserved functional association between bactofilins and M23 peptidases.
evidence: This is an inference from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: H. neptunium LmdC is a predicted bitopic membrane protein with a short N-terminal cytoplasmic region, a transmembrane helix, large periplasmic region composed of a predicted coiled-coil domain, and a C-terminal M23 peptidase domain.
source: Like many of its homologs, H. neptunium LmdC is a predicted bitopic membrane protein with a short N-terminal cytoplasmic region, a transmembrane helix, large periplasmic region composed of a predicted coiled-coil domain, and a C-terminal M23 peptidase domain (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a prediction from bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Members of the M23 peptidase family usually have Zn+-dependent hydrolase activity and cleave bonds within the peptide side chains of the peptidoglycan meshwork.
source: Members of the M23 peptidase family usually have Zn+-dependent hydrolase activity and cleave bonds within the peptide side chains of the peptidoglycan meshwork (Firczuk et al., 2005; Grabowska et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about M23 peptidases supported by citations.

claim: There are various M23 peptidase representatives that have lost their enzymatic activity because of mutations in residues required for metal cofactor binding and have instead adopted regulatory roles in cell wall biosynthesis.
source: However, there are also various representatives that have lost their enzymatic activity because of mutations in residues required for metal cofactor binding and have instead adopted regulatory roles in cell wall biosynthesis (Figueroa-Cuilan et al., 2021; Goley et al., 2010; Gurnani Serrano et al., 2021; Möll et al., 2010; Poggio et al., 2010; Uehara et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about M23 peptidases supported by multiple citations.

claim: The M23 peptidase domain of LmdC features all residues reported to be critical for Zn2+ binding.
source: An amino acid alignment showed that the M23 peptidase domain of LmdC features all residues reported to be critical for Zn2+ binding, suggesting that it could act as a genuine peptidoglycan hydrolase (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignment shown in Figure 8B.

claim: LmdC could act as a genuine peptidoglycan hydrolase.
source: An amino acid alignment showed that the M23 peptidase domain of LmdC features all residues reported to be critical for Zn2+ binding, suggesting that it could act as a genuine peptidoglycan hydrolase (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an inference from the sequence alignment.

claim: In a structural model of LmdC generated with AlphaFold2, the periplasmic coiled-coil and M23 peptidase domains form an elongated, rigid unit with two flanking non-structured regions that is flexibly linked to the transmembrane helix.
source: In a structural model of LmdC generated with AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021), the periplasmic coiled-coil and M23 peptidase domains form an elongated, rigid unit with two flanking non-structured regions that is flexibly linked to the transmembrane helix (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling (AlphaFold2) shown in Figure 8C.

claim: LmdC homologs form a distinct clade among the M23 peptidases that is broadly conserved among species but particularly enriched in alpha- and deltaproteobacteria.
source: Notably, LmdC homologs were shown to form a distinct clade among the M23 peptidases that is broadly conserved among species but particularly enriched in alpha- and deltaproteobacteria (Figueroa-Cuilan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Figueroa-Cuilan et al., 2021).

claim: Upon treatment with the M23 peptidase domain of LmdC, the relative proportion of dimeric muropeptide species (Tetra-Tetra and Tetra-Penta) strongly decreased.
source: Upon treatment with the protein, the relative proportion of dimeric muropeptide species (Tetra-Tetra and Tetra-Penta) strongly decreased, regardless of the length of the crosslinked peptides and without the formation of major additional monomer peaks (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an observation from in vitro peptidoglycan hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The activity of LmdC was particularly high at a pH value of 5.
source: The activity of LmdC was particularly high at a pH value of 5, but the physiological significance of this effect remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an observation from in vitro peptidoglycan hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 8D.

claim: LmdC is a DD-endopeptidase cleaving the bond between the meso-diaminopimelic acid residue of one peptide and D-alanine at position 4 of the other peptide.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that LmdC is a DD-endopeptidase cleaving the bond between the meso-diaminopimelic acid residue of one peptide and D-alanine at position 4 of the other peptide, thereby reducing the degree of cross-linkage within the peptidoglycan layer (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the in vitro peptidoglycan hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: LmdC reduces the degree of cross-linkage within the peptidoglycan layer.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that LmdC is a DD-endopeptidase cleaving the bond between the meso-diaminopimelic acid residue of one peptide and D-alanine at position 4 of the other peptide, thereby reducing the degree of cross-linkage within the peptidoglycan layer (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed cleavage specificity.

claim: All attempts to delete the lmdC gene or the entire putative lmdC-bacA operon or to generate non-functional truncated lmdC alleles were unsuccessful.
source: However, all attempts to delete the lmdC gene or the entire putative lmdC-bacA operon or to generate non-functional truncated lmdC alleles were unsuccessful, in line with a previous report suggesting that lmdC is essential for viability (Cserti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation from genetic manipulation attempts, consistent with a cited study.

claim: lmdC is essential for viability in H. neptunium.
source: However, all attempts to delete the lmdC gene or the entire putative lmdC-bacA operon or to generate non-functional truncated lmdC alleles were unsuccessful, in line with a previous report suggesting that lmdC is essential for viability (Cserti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the inability to delete the gene, supported by a cited study.

claim: It was not possible to generate a conditional lmdC mutant producing the gene under the control of a copper-inducible promoter.
source: It was also not possible to generate a conditional lmdC mutant producing the gene under the control of a copper-inducible promoter, suggesting that its expression level needs to be precisely regulated.
evidence: This is an observation from genetic manipulation attempts.

claim: The expression level of lmdC needs to be precisely regulated.
source: It was also not possible to generate a conditional lmdC mutant producing the gene under the control of a copper-inducible promoter, suggesting that its expression level needs to be precisely regulated.
evidence: This is an inference from the inability to generate a conditional mutant.

claim: Induction with copper led to the formation of an sgRNA-dCas9 complex that targeted the non-coding strand of lmdC, generating a road-block that prevented the movement of RNA polymerase and, thus, gene expression.
source: Induction with copper led to the formation of an sgRNA-dCas9 complex that targeted the non-coding strand of lmdC, generating a road-block that prevented the movement of RNA polymerase and, thus, gene expression (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: This is a description of the CRISPRi mechanism, supported by immunoblot data in Figure 9D.

claim: The block of lmdC expression led to cell shape defects very similar to those observed for the ΔbacA mutant.
source: Importantly, the block of lmdC expression led to cell shape defects very similar to those observed for the ΔbacA mutant, as reflected by a large proportion of distorted and amorphous cells, which still showed close-to-normal growth rates (Figure 9E and F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from CRISPRi experiments shown in Figure 9E and F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Cells depleted of LmdC showed close-to-normal growth rates despite cell shape defects.
source: Importantly, the block of lmdC expression led to cell shape defects very similar to those observed for the ΔbacA mutant, as reflected by a large proportion of distorted and amorphous cells, which still showed close-to-normal growth rates (Figure 9E and F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from CRISPRi experiments shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Induced cells of a control strain carrying the empty pdCas9Entry plasmid did not show any obvious phenotype.
source: Induced cells of a control strain carrying the empty pdCas9Entry plasmid did not show any obvious phenotype, indicating that the presence of dCas9 alone did not have any adverse effects on cell growth or viability (Figure 9D and E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from control experiments shown in Figure 9D and E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The presence of dCas9 alone did not have any adverse effects on cell growth or viability.
source: Induced cells of a control strain carrying the empty pdCas9Entry plasmid did not show any obvious phenotype, indicating that the presence of dCas9 alone did not have any adverse effects on cell growth or viability (Figure 9D and E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference from the control experiments.

claim: LmdC and BacA are part of the same morphogenetic pathway.
source: These results suggest that LmdC and BacA are part of the same morphogenetic pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the similar phenotypes of ΔbacA and LmdC-depleted cells.

claim: BacA interacts with the LmdC peptide with an apparent equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of ~15 µM.
source: The results showed that BacA interacts with the LmdC peptide with an apparent equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of ~15 µM.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from bio-layer interferometry experiments shown in Figure 9G and H.

claim: An unrelated peptide used as a negative control was not bound by BacA with appreciable affinity.
source: By contrast, an unrelated peptide used as a negative control was not bound with appreciable affinity (Figure 9G and H).
evidence: This is an observation from bio-layer interferometry experiments shown in Figure 9G and H.

claim: BacA and LmdC interact directly.
source: This result confirms a direct interaction between BacA and LmdC and identifies the N-terminal cytoplasmic region of LmdC as the interaction determinant for BacA association.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the bio-layer interferometry experiments.

claim: The N-terminal cytoplasmic region of LmdC is the interaction determinant for BacA association.
source: This result confirms a direct interaction between BacA and LmdC and identifies the N-terminal cytoplasmic region of LmdC as the interaction determinant for BacA association.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the bio-layer interferometry experiments using an N-terminal LmdC peptide.

claim: R. rubrum contains a putative lmdC-bacA operon similar to that in H. neptunium.
source: To further explore this possibility, we turned our efforts to the spiral-shaped bacterium Rhodospirillum rubrum, which contains a putative lmdC-bacA operon similar to that in H. neptunium (Munk et al., 2011; Figure 10A).
evidence: This is an observation from genomic analysis shown in Figure 10A, with a citation.

claim: The R. rubrum BacA homolog Rru_A1867 (BacARs) is 37% identical (57% similar) to BacA of H. neptunium.
source: The R. rubrum BacA homolog Rru_A1867 (BacARs) is 37% identical (57% similar) to BacA of H. neptunium and also consists of a central Bactofilin A/B domain flanked by terminal non-structured regions (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison shown in Figure 10B.

claim: BacARs consists of a central Bactofilin A/B domain flanked by terminal non-structured regions.
source: The R. rubrum BacA homolog Rru_A1867 (BacARs) is 37% identical (57% similar) to BacA of H. neptunium and also consists of a central Bactofilin A/B domain flanked by terminal non-structured regions (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a result from structural prediction shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The LmdC homolog Rru_A1868 (LmdCRs) is 39% identical (55% similar) to H. neptunium LmdC.
source: The LmdC homolog Rru_A1868 (LmdCRs) is 39% identical (55% similar) to H. neptunium LmdC and has a similar predicted molecular structure (Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from sequence comparison, with a citation for the structural prediction.

claim: LmdCRs has a similar predicted molecular structure to H. neptunium LmdC.
source: The LmdC homolog Rru_A1868 (LmdCRs) is 39% identical (55% similar) to H. neptunium LmdC and has a similar predicted molecular structure (Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a result from structural prediction cited to Varadi et al., 2022.

claim: The deletion of bacARs led to a noticeable increase in cell curvature.
source: The deletion of bacARs led to a noticeable increase in cell curvature (Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), as also reflected in a significant increase in cell sinuosity (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 10C, D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The deletion of bacARs led to a significant increase in cell sinuosity.
source: The deletion of bacARs led to a noticeable increase in cell curvature (Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), as also reflected in a significant increase in cell sinuosity (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cell sinuosity measurements shown in Figure 10D.

claim: A very similar effect on cell curvature was observed for cells lacking lmdCRs or both bacARs and lmdCRs.
source: A very similar effect was observed for cells lacking lmdCRs or both bacARs and lmdCRs, indicating that the two gene products act in the same pathway and jointly contribute to cell shape maintenance in R. rubrum (Figure 10C and D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 10C, D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The two gene products BacARs and LmdCRs act in the same pathway and jointly contribute to cell shape maintenance in R. rubrum.
source: A very similar effect was observed for cells lacking lmdCRs or both bacARs and lmdCRs, indicating that the two gene products act in the same pathway and jointly contribute to cell shape maintenance in R. rubrum (Figure 10C and D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference from the similar phenotypes of the mutants.

claim: In the R. rubrum ΔbacARs and ΔlmdCRs mutant strains, the global composition of peptidoglycan was largely unchanged.
source: In the two mutant strains, the global composition of peptidoglycan was largely unchanged, supporting the notion that the BacARs-LmdCRs pathway modifies the cell wall only locally or acts by modulating the activity of the standard cell elongation machinery (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an observation from muropeptide analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The BacARs-LmdCRs pathway modifies the cell wall only locally or acts by modulating the activity of the standard cell elongation machinery.
source: In the two mutant strains, the global composition of peptidoglycan was largely unchanged, supporting the notion that the BacARs-LmdCRs pathway modifies the cell wall only locally or acts by modulating the activity of the standard cell elongation machinery (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the unchanged global peptidoglycan composition.

claim: BacARs-CHY and LmdCNRs-mNG were consistently localized to the same subcellular positions, forming patchy or filamentous structures that were preferentially, but not exclusively, positioned at the inner curve of the cell.
source: We found that BacARs-CHY and LmdCNRs-mNG were consistently localized to the same subcellular positions, forming patchy or filamentous structures that were preferentially, but not exclusively, positioned at the inner curve of the cell (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 10E.

claim: A very similar localization behavior was observed for BacARs-CHY and LmdCNRs-mNG in the presence of wild-type LmdCRs.
source: A very similar behavior was observed in the presence of wild-type LmdCRs (Figure 10—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Cells consistently displayed higher signal intensities of BacARs-CHY and LmdCNRs-mNG at the inner curve.
source: In both cases, cells consistently displayed higher signal intensities at the inner curve (Figure 10F and G), supporting the notion that BacARs-LmdCRs assemblies promote cell wall biosynthesis in the inner curve to reduce overall cell curvature.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fluorescence intensity analysis shown in Figure 10F and G.

claim: BacARs-LmdCRs assemblies promote cell wall biosynthesis in the inner curve to reduce overall cell curvature.
source: In both cases, cells consistently displayed higher signal intensities at the inner curve (Figure 10F and G), supporting the notion that BacARs-LmdCRs assemblies promote cell wall biosynthesis in the inner curve to reduce overall cell curvature.
evidence: This is an inference from the localization pattern and mutant phenotypes.

claim: A BacARs-mNG fusion showed a reduced enrichment in the absence of LmdCRs.
source: Notably, a BacARs-mNG fusion showed a reduced enrichment in the absence of LmdCRs, whereas LmdCNRs-mNG completely lost its asymmetric distribution in the ΔbacARs background (Figure 10H–J).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 10H–J.

claim: LmdCNRs-mNG completely lost its asymmetric distribution in the ΔbacARs background.
source: Notably, a BacARs-mNG fusion showed a reduced enrichment in the absence of LmdCRs, whereas LmdCNRs-mNG completely lost its asymmetric distribution in the ΔbacARs background (Figure 10H–J).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 10H–J.

claim: BacARs polymers act as recruitment platforms for LmdCRs.
source: These results identify BacARs polymers as recruitment platforms for LmdCRs, although an interaction between the two proteins appears to be required for normal BacARs localization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localization dependencies observed in the mutants.

claim: An interaction between BacARs and LmdCRs appears to be required for normal BacARs localization.
source: These results identify BacARs polymers as recruitment platforms for LmdCRs, although an interaction between the two proteins appears to be required for normal BacARs localization.
evidence: This is an inference from the reduced enrichment of BacARs in the absence of LmdCRs.

claim: The N-terminal cytoplasmic region of LmdCRs contains a β-hairpin motif that is conserved among LmdC homologs.
source: The N-terminal cytoplasmic region of LmdCRs contains a β-hairpin motif (Figure 11A) that is conserved among LmdC homologs.
evidence: This is an observation from structural prediction and sequence analysis shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Modifications in cluster I (R25, H26, L27) of the β-hairpin motif completely abolished the enrichment of LmdC at the inner curve of the cell.
source: The modifications in cluster I completely abolished the enrichment of LmdC at the inner curve of the cell, indicating that the β-hairpin motif is a critical part of the BacA binding site (Figure 11C and D).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy of mutant strains shown in Figure 11C and D.

claim: The β-hairpin motif is a critical part of the BacA binding site.
source: The modifications in cluster I completely abolished the enrichment of LmdC at the inner curve of the cell, indicating that the β-hairpin motif is a critical part of the BacA binding site (Figure 11C and D).
evidence: This is an inference from the loss of localization upon mutation.

claim: The loss of interaction between BacARs and LmdCRs (cluster I mutant) led to a reduced inner-curve enrichment of BacARs-CHY.
source: Notably, the loss of interaction between the two proteins also led to a reduced inner-curve enrichment of BacARs-CHY, as previously observed in the ΔlmdCRs background (Figure 10I and J).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy of mutant strains shown in Figure 11C and D.

claim: LmdCRs binding is required for BacA to adopt its proper spatial organization.
source: This observation confirms that LmdCRs binding is required for BacA to adopt its proper spatial organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localization dependencies observed in the mutants.

claim: Similar defects were caused by the modification of cluster II (R30, S31).
source: Similar defects were caused by the modification of cluster II (Figure 11C and E).
evidence: This is an observation from fluorescence microscopy of mutant strains shown in Figure 11C and E.

claim: The cluster II mutant protein may still show a residual, yet aberrant interaction with BacARs that has a negative effect on BacARs localization.
source: However, in this case, BacARs-CHY was also no longer enriched at the inner curve, suggesting that the mutant protein may still show a residual, yet aberrant interaction with BacARs that has a negative effect on BacARs localization.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the localization pattern of the cluster II mutant.

claim: Bactofilins and LmdC-like M23 peptidases form a conserved morphogenetic module that is involved in the establishment of complex bacterial cell shapes.
source: Collectively, these findings confirm a functional association between the bactofilin cytoskeleton and LmdCRs in R. rubrum. Moreover, they support the notion that bactofilins and LmdC-like M23 peptidases form a conserved morphogenetic module that is involved in the establishment of complex bacterial cell shapes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined results in H. neptunium and R. rubrum.
